---
title: Choosing and configuring engines
---

## Overview

When Quarto renders a document that contains executable code, it hands that
code to an **engine** — knitr, Jupyter, or an engine supplied by an
extension. Most documents never mention an engine at all: Quarto looks at the
languages of the executable cells and picks engines for you. Two metadata
keys let you take control when you need it, and they divide the work cleanly
between them:

- **`engine:`** names *which engines are at play* in a document — the
  execution sequence.
- **`engines:`** configures *how engines behave*, whichever ones end up at
  play, without naming any.

The keys are one letter apart and easy to confuse, so it helps to keep one
question in mind. When you are picking participants, reach for `engine:`.
When you are adjusting the behavior of a participant that resolution might
pick on its own, reach for `engines:`.

## `engine:` — naming the engines at play

A document's `engine:` key declares its **execution sequence**: the engines
that will run, in the order they will run. The key accepts three shapes.

```{.yaml filename="document.qmd"}
engine: knitr                  # a one-engine sequence

engine: [knitr, jupyter]       # two engines, run in this order

engine:
  - jupyter:                   # an entry with configuration:
      kernel: python3          # the map's value is passed to the engine
```

Because `engine:` *names participants*, writing it is a committal act — Quarto
treats your list as the complete statement of who plays. Three consequences
follow:

1. **The implicit-fallback safety net turns off.** Normally, a computational
   language that no engine claims falls to Jupyter (or to any engine that
   declares a stronger fallback claim). An explicit `engine:` list disables
   that net: if your list does not cover a language, no unlisted engine is
   quietly added to cover it. To opt out of execution entirely, write
   `engine: markdown`.
2. **Listed engines are present by declaration.** Some engines extend their
   reach only when they are already in play — knitr's reticulate taking
   `{python}` cells, for example. Listing an engine makes it present, even in
   a document where it wins no language on its own.
3. **Order is execution order.** Engines run one after another, each
   consuming the previous engine's output, so an engine that generates code
   must be listed before the engine that executes what it generates.

`engine:` is read from **merged metadata**, so a project-level `engine:` in
`_quarto.yml` also participates and concatenates with a document's own list.
When both layers name the same engine, the project's entry wins; see
[Precedence and overrides](#precedence-and-overrides) below for how a
document overrides that.

## `engines:` — configuring engines without naming any

The project-level `engines:` key configures the **pool of engines** that
resolution draws from — the built-ins plus any discovered extensions.
Writing it never puts an engine into play. Its guarantees mirror the
consequences of `engine:`, which is exactly what makes it safe to set
project-wide:

- it never makes any document's sequence explicit — the implicit-fallback net
  stays on;
- it never makes an engine "present," so it triggers no reach-extending side
  effects;
- it never causes an engine to run that would not have run anyway.

The key is an array whose entries come in three forms:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
engines:
  - knitr                      # a bare name: influences ordering only
  - legacy-python:             # a name-keyed map: per-engine configuration;
      claims: [python]         # `claims` is the configuration this key accepts
```

The one selection-adjacent influence `engines:` keeps is **ordering**. The
order engines are visited in breaks ties between equal-strength claims, and it
sets the order in which the chosen engines run. So `engines:` never *casts*
anyone — claims decide who runs — it only shapes the order of whoever the
claims chose.

## Claim tables

A **claim table** is the configuration an `engines:` entry (or an `engine:`
entry) can carry: it declares which languages an engine handles. This is the
mechanism behind the headline feature below, so it is worth understanding on
its own first.

Its simplest form is a list of languages, each of which the engine then
claims as its own:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
engines:
  - my-engine:
      claims: [r, python]      # my-engine handles both r and python
```

For finer control, write the table as a map from language to a claim object.
The `kind` field says *how* the engine wants the language:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
engines:
  - my-engine:
      claims:
        r: {kind: primary}     # r is mine to execute
        python: interop        # concise sugar for {kind: interop}
        julia: true            # shorthand for {kind: primary}
        sql: 2                 # shorthand for a primary claim at priority 2
```

A bare kind name (`primary`, `interop`, or `fallback`) is concise sugar for
`{kind: <name>}` when you don't need `priority` or `whenClass`. The three
kinds are:

- **`primary`** — the engine executes this language. This is the default, and
  what every entry in the list-shorthand form becomes.
- **`interop`** — the engine takes this language *only when it is already in
  play* for another reason. This is how knitr picks up `{python}` via
  reticulate without dragging knitr into a Python-only document.
- **`fallback`** — the engine is a catch-all for anything unclaimed. Jupyter
  is the built-in universal fallback; any engine can declare its own with a
  bare `fallback:` entry, which claims everything at the fallback floor:

  ```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
  engines:
    - my-engine:
        claims:
          fallback: {priority: 0}
  ```

### A table replaces, it does not merge

A claim table is a **whole-table replacement**: it stands in for the engine's
*entire* claim surface, not a patch on top of it. A language absent from the
table is simply not claimed. This gives two useful moves.

**Masking.** Because a table replaces everything, omitting a language removes
a claim the engine would otherwise make. To stop knitr from grabbing your
Python cells via reticulate across a whole project, give it a table that
claims only R:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
engines:
  - knitr:
      claims: [r]              # knitr keeps r; its interop on python is gone
```

**The empty-table mask.** An empty table claims nothing at all. Applied to
Jupyter, it switches off the universal fallback project-wide:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
engines:
  - jupyter:
      claims: []               # jupyter now claims nothing
```

### Conditional claims with `whenClass`

A claim can be gated on a cell's first class, so an engine takes a language
only in a specific spelling. A marimo engine, for instance, wants
`{python .marimo}` cells but should leave plain `{python}` cells alone:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
engines:
  - marimo:
      claims:
        python: {kind: primary, whenClass: marimo}
```

With this table, `{python .marimo}` resolves to marimo and a plain `{python}`
cell does not — it falls through to whichever engine claims Python normally.

## Making a legacy extension resolvable {#backward-compatibility}

This is the payoff the two keys were designed for.

An engine extension can declare its claims statically in its own
`_extension.yml`, which lets Quarto resolve documents without ever loading the
extension's code. Older extensions predate this and declare no static claims —
so Quarto cannot know what they handle without loading them, and tools that
resolve engines ahead of time (such as the language server) cannot see them.

You do not need to edit the extension to fix this. Supply its claim table in
your project's `engines:` key, and Quarto answers the extension's language
claims from your table alone:

```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"}
engines:
  - legacy-python:
      claims: [python]         # declare what the extension handles
```

With that one block, every document in the project resolves ahead of time,
the extension is never loaded merely to answer a claim, and the extension
itself is untouched.

## Declaring generated languages

Quarto decides the engine sequence from the languages it finds in a
document's source. An engine that *generates* code in another language poses
a problem: the target language has no cell in the source yet, so no engine is
lined up to own it.

The `generated-languages` key closes that gap. List the languages a document
will emit, and each one gets an owner in the sequence before any cell of that
language exists:

```{.yaml filename="document.qmd"}
generated-languages: [python, sql]
```

The key is a flat list, declared once at the top level. It only widens the
scan when the document already has executable cells of its own; a document
with no code cells stays plain Markdown regardless of what it lists here.

## Precedence and overrides

Two different rules govern conflicts, depending on what is in conflict.

**Claim tables are document-authoritative.** When a document's own
`engine:`-entry table and the project's `engines:` table both cover the same
engine, the *document's* table wins — a document knows its own languages
better than the project does.

**Engine configuration and sequence are project-first.** For the engine
sequence and for non-claims configuration such as a kernel name, the project
layer wins on conflict, following Quarto's normal metadata merge. A document
that needs to override the project's choice says so explicitly with the
`!prefer` merge tag:

```{.yaml filename="document.qmd"}
engine: !prefer [jupyter]      # this document's sequence wins over the project's
```
